summary: Comments on the File Transfer Protocol, proposing design changes and slight modifications. It replaces the earlier discussion in RFC 607 and is related to RFCs 614, 542 and 640.

eli5.summary: This is a cleaned-up list of ideas to improve the file-transfer rules, replacing an earlier list.

why does ftp use reply codes
subtitle: Twelve proposed fixes to the 1974 File Transfer Protocol, from command names to reply codes.

tldr.problem: The File Transfer Protocol of RFC 542 had drawbacks that made life hard for people writing FTP user and server programs.
tldr.mechanism: The authors list twelve problems, each with a proposed solution, such as four-letter verbs, one success digit and a fixed code for continuation lines.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of comments, not a specification, and it replaces the draft that was released by mistake as RFC 607.

today: This RFC replaces RFC 607 and comments on the protocol of RFC 542. Its status is listed as Unknown, and the text does not say which proposals were adopted.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
This document replaces RFC 607, which was released by mistake while still a rough draft. The authors ask readers to disregard RFC 607 and treat this one as their accurate opinion.

They say the File Transfer Protocol of RFC 542 has serious drawbacks. Some are basic and imply large design changes, which a later RFC will discuss. Others could be fixed with little effort, and those are listed here.
sections.eli5: The first list was sent out too early by accident, so this is the proper, cleaned-up list.

sections.title: Small Fixes to Commands and Handshakes
sections.content:
Items 1 to 5 deal with how commands behave. A new ACTV command would make a passive server active again, because REIN affects more than that one state. The three-letter verb BYE would become a four-letter one such as QUIT, with all future verbs also four letters, since fixed-length strings are easier to handle.

The order of the handshake after a transfer command is unspecified. The server should send the 250 reply before trying to open the data connection, and any login or file-access checks must come first. A server that does not support a command because it is not needed must return the success reply. Finally, maximum lengths should be set for command lines, replies, user names, passwords, account numbers and pathnames, after a poll of serving sites.
sections.eli5: The authors want shorter, same-size command words, a clear order for the greetings, and size limits so programs know how much space to reserve.

sections.title: Simplifying Reply Codes
sections.content:
Items 6 to 11 deal with replies. Continuation lines of a multi-line reply may start with arbitrary text, and replies may be nested, which makes decoding hard. The proposal is a unique numeric code such as 009 on every line after the first, or at least no nested replies, or a stated maximum nesting level.

Different commands also use different success codes, so the first digit does not reliably mean success. For example, a good USER gives 230 and a good BYTE gives 200, while 100 means success for STAT. The authors propose that every successful command return a code starting with one digit, such as 2, and that finer detail ride in the later digits. They also ask for clearer reply descriptions and for the connection greeting codes 300 and 020 to be put in consistent series.
sections.eli5: Right now a yes can look like many different numbers. They want every yes to start the same way so a program can tell quickly.

sections.title: A Likely Typo and Reply 332
sections.content: Item 12 notes that reply code 332 LOGIN PLEASE is missing from the command-reply table. It would make sense as a more-information-needed reply for all commands that require a login. The authors stress that 332 should be used for this, since many servers use other codes, such as 451 and 504, to mean the same thing.
sections.eli5: One message that means please log in is missing from the table, and servers have been using different numbers for it.

references.text: Comments on the File Transfer Protocol, RFC 607.
